 Southern California's wild weather swings continue. Next up, rain
 Lucas Brady Woods 
 covers the weather and disasters, among other climate and science topics.
 Published October 20, 2026 at 3:08 PM PDT
 Rain is expected Wednesday night and Thursday morning across Southern California. It will be the first cold storm of the rainy season. ( Apu Gomes / AFP via Getty Images )
 One year ago, Congress defunded public media. Now that we're 100% community funded, please become a sustaining member or increase your existing membership today .
 Listen
 0:42
 Cold storm moving in 
 This will be a change from the muggy tropical storms Southern California experienced this summer. 
 Southern California is likely in for a solid dose of rain this week, just days after heat and Santa Ana winds helped fuel several wildfires across the region .
 Forecasters expect the bulk of the rain to roll into the Los Angeles basin Wednesday night and continue into Thursday morning, with a small chance of thunderstorms and hail.
 The San Fernando Valley, San Gabriel Valley and coastal areas across L.A. and Orange counties could get around an inch over the next few days. Hills and mountains could get up to 3 inches.
 “We could see some pretty high rain rates,” said National Weather Service meteorologist Mike Wofford. “It's a good storm for this time of year — it's a little stronger than what we would see normally.”
 More news
 United Nations report highlights significant increase in US climate pollution 
 The U.S. is the only major economy where planet-warming pollution dramatically increased last year. The United Nations warns the planet is on track for catastrophic warming.
 Researchers project SoCal’s climate extremes will worsen in coming decades 
 The region is bracing for more extreme heat, beach erosion and drought that could be here within two decades, according to a new assessment by the state.
 Eaton Fire homeowners can now apply for free soil testing and cleanup. Here's how. 
 Program will prioritize households with pregnant people, young kids, older adults and people with disabilities
 The possibility of significant rain in the mountains raises concerns about flooding in areas recently burned in wildfires, particularly around the Bryson Fire burn scar near Malibu, which is only a few days old. Burn scars can’t absorb heavy rainfall and are susceptible to landslides.
 The National Weather Service has issued a flood watch for the Santa Monica Mountains and surrounding communities from Wednesday afternoon through Thursday. That means heavy rain there could flood streets, creeks and rivers. The flood watch area includes both the Bryson Fire and Palisades Fire burn scars.
 This will also be the first nontropical storm of the season, meaning it’s moving into the region from the north. Most storms that hit Southern California follow a similar path, especially during the winter, unlike the tropical storms that formed off the coast of Mexico and brought muggy weather to the region this summer.
 Sponsored message 
 Nontropical storms also bring cold air to the region. On Wednesday and Thursday, forecasters expect highs in the 60s and 70s. High elevations will be even cooler.

LAist is now 100% community funded and that means we’re taking our future into our own hands and turning to you to keep local reporting strong.
You come to LAist because you want independent reporting and trustworthy local information. Our nonprofit newsroom doesn’t answer to shareholders looking to turn a profit. Instead,  we answer to you and our communities. We are free to follow facts wherever they lead and to hold power to account without fear or favor. Our only loyalty is to our readers and listeners and our mission: to inform, engage, and strengthen Southern California’s communities.
